svg.title: Richmond's lines, 1871 to 1977: ordinances, the 1937 map, and what was built and cleared on graded land
svg.desc: 1871: The city's wards are redrawn to pack Black voters into one, Jackson Ward. (Library of Virginia, Mapping Inequality timeline) 1888: Electric streetcars open suburbs that covenants keep white. (Library of Virginia) April 1911: City Council passes a residential segregation ordinance. In 1912 the General Assembly lets every Virginia city do the same. (Library of Virginia; Encyclopedia Virginia) 1917: In Buchanan v. Warley the Supreme Court strikes down segregation ordinances. (Library of Virginia) 1924 or 1929: Richmond passes a new ordinance tied to the state's Racial Integrity Act. A federal appeals court strikes it down in 1929. (Encyclopedia Virginia gives 1924; the Library of Virginia gives 1929) 1933: Congress creates the Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC) to refinance home mortgages in default. (Home Owners' Loan Act, June 13, 1933 (Wikipedia); Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, 2022) April 3, 1937: The HOLC's map of Richmond grades its residential areas A to D. (National Archives, RG 195, via FRASER) 1943: Gilpin Court is dedicated on cleared Apostle Town land in D1. (Library of Virginia, Craig, 2025; Encyclopedia Virginia) 1946: Harland Bartholomew's master plan calls the city's Black neighborhoods slums. (Encyclopedia Virginia) 1948: In Shelley v. Kraemer the Supreme Court makes racial covenants unenforceable. (Library of Virginia) 1955–1958: The Richmond–Petersburg Turnpike, now I-95 and I-64, is cut through D1. By 1957 about 1,900 Black families had been displaced. (Encyclopedia Virginia, citing the Richmond Times-Dispatch; the Jackson Ward story) 1962: Mosby Court opens in D5, home to many of the 1,300 people the 17th Street renewal displaced. (Encyclopedia Virginia) 1967–1970: A study calls Fulton (D7) a slum; the 1970 plan would displace about 785 households. (Encyclopedia Virginia) 1970: Richmond annexes 23 square miles of Chesterfield County. Public housing, 464 scattered-site units, is built in Blackwell (D11.5). (Library of Virginia; Richmond Magazine, 2018) 1973: HUD approves the Randolph project (D8), about 1,800 to be displaced, for the Downtown Expressway. (Encyclopedia Virginia)
